definition: The artificial intelligence industry in Canada is a rapidly expanding sector.
details: Although Canada held a pioneering role in the early development of artificial intelligence, transforming research excellence into broad commercial adoption has proven challenging. Despite globally recognized scientific achievements and a deep pool of skilled experts, by June 2024, Canada recorded the lowest rate of AI integration among OECD countries, with only 12% of firms implementing AI in their products or services. However, AI adoption has shown significant momentum—doubling from mid-2024 to mid-2025, rising from 6.1% to 12.2%. As of September 2025, Statistics Canada indicated that while about one-third of Canadian businesses had no plans to adopt artificial intelligence in the next year, 14.5% reported intentions to begin using AI for producing goods or delivering services. The primary reasons for not moving forward with AI were lack of relevance, insufficient knowledge, and privacy concerns. According to Public Works Canada (PwC), the pace of AI adoption in Canada is roughly three-quarters of the United States rate, highlighting a notable gap between the two countries in business integration of this technology. explainer.lead: Canada’s AI industry spans pioneering research, skilled experts, and businesses turning that work into products and services. Its central challenge is commercial adoption: Canadian firms have generally integrated AI more slowly than their scientific reputation might suggest.

tiers.eli5: Canada is a bit like a student who is excellent at inventing things in science class but slower to use those inventions in everyday shops. Its AI adoption recently doubled, yet many businesses still see no need for it, do not know enough about it, or worry about privacy.
tiers.practitioner: For an engineer, this is less a technology than the environment in which AI projects are funded, built, and deployed. Adoption work should start with a relevant business use case, then address knowledge gaps and privacy concerns rather than treating a model demonstration as commercial integration.
tiers.paperLevel: The sector can be summarized as research capability -> commercialization -> firm-level AI integration, with adoption used as an observable outcome. Reported firm adoption rose from 6.1% in mid-2024 to 12.2% in mid-2025; these figures should not be conflated with the separate June 2024 OECD comparison, and the evidence does not establish why adoption increased.

explainer.example: In a hypothetical group of 1,000 firms, the reported mid-2024 adoption rate of 6.1% corresponds to 61 firms using AI. At the mid-2025 rate of 12.2%, the equivalent count would be 122 firms, illustrating the reported doubling without implying that these were the same firms.

explainer.intuition: Scientific leadership and commercial adoption are different achievements: a country can produce excellent AI research while many of its businesses remain unsure whether, or how, to use it.
howItWorks: Researchers and skilled experts develop AI knowledge and techniques.
Businesses identify relevant uses in their products or services.
They address practical barriers such as insufficient knowledge and privacy concerns.
Firms integrate AI into the production of goods or delivery of services.
Business surveys track adoption and reveal the remaining gap between research strength and widespread use.
explainer.whyItMatters: Commercial adoption determines how broadly research excellence reaches everyday goods and services. Canada’s recent momentum matters, but its gap with the United States and the substantial share of firms with no adoption plans show that diffusion remains incomplete.
misconceptions: Pioneering AI research does not automatically mean that most Canadian businesses use AI.
Planning to adopt AI is not the same as having already integrated it.
The doubling from 6.1% to 12.2% does not mean that every measurement of Canadian adoption uses the same baseline or survey definition.
